summary: This standards-track document describes the Segment Routing architecture, which uses source routing. A node steers a packet through an ordered list of instructions called segments, which can represent topological or service-based instructions. A segment may have local meaning to a node or global meaning in the domain.

plainLanguage.summary: Segment Routing lets the sending edge steer a packet with an ordered list of instructions. Routers process the active instruction as the packet moves through the network.

questions: how does source routing with segments work
how does segment routing keep state
subtitle: A source-routing architecture that puts an ordered list of network instructions into each packet.

tldr.problem: Explicitly steering a flow through a chosen path can require each router along that path to keep per-flow state.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress attaches an ordered list of segments, or instructions, to the packet. SR-MPLS encodes them as labels; SRv6 encodes them as IPv6 addresses in a routing header.
tldr.outcome: The architecture keeps per-flow state at the ingress nodes and assumes a trusted domain with filtering at its boundaries. RFC 8402 has been updated by RFC 9256.

today: RFC 8402 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9256. Its security model assumes a trusted domain and requires filtering at its boundaries.

sections.title: Source Routing with Segments
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) uses an ordered list of instructions called segments to steer a packet. A segment can describe a route through the network, a service to apply, or a quality-of-service treatment. A segment can be local to one router or global within an SR domain.

An SR Policy is the segment list used by a headend to steer packets. The architecture allows explicit per-flow paths while keeping per-flow state only at ingress nodes. It defines objects and behavior, while other documents specify implementation details.
sections.plainLanguage: The ingress router adds a list of instructions that describes how to steer a packet. Each router acts on the instruction that is active when the packet reaches it.

sections.title: Local and Global Segments
sections.content:
A segment identifier (SID) names a segment. The SR domain is the set of nodes participating in the source-routing model, generally under one administrative authority.

The active segment is the instruction a router processes. The operations are PUSH, which adds a segment; NEXT, which makes the following segment active after the current one is complete; and CONTINUE, which keeps the current segment active.

The SR Global Block identifies global segments in a domain. The SR Local Block reserves identifiers for local segments. For SR-MPLS, the RFC strongly recommends using the same SRGB across nodes so a label identifies the same global segment.
sections.plainLanguage: A segment is an instruction, and a SID identifies it. PUSH adds an instruction, NEXT advances to the next one, and CONTINUE keeps the current one active.

sections.title: SR-MPLS and SRv6 Data Planes
sections.content:
SR-MPLS uses the existing MPLS forwarding plane. A segment is an MPLS label, the policy is a label stack, and the top label is active. When a segment completes, its label is popped.

SRv6 uses a new IPv6 routing header. A segment is an IPv6 address, and the header contains the ordered list. The active segment is the packet's destination address; a pointer in the routing header indicates the next one. When a segment completes, the pointer advances and the next address becomes the destination.

An operator must explicitly instantiate an SRv6 SID. An ordinary IPv6 node address is not automatically a segment.
sections.plainLanguage: SR-MPLS carries the instruction list as labels. SRv6 carries addresses in a routing header and updates the packet's destination as it advances.

sections.title: Segments Advertised by Link-State Routing
sections.content:
A link-state IGP can advertise segments for prefixes and adjacencies. A Prefix-SID identifies a route to a prefix under a selected algorithm. The RFC defines shortest-path forwarding and Strict-SPF, which requires routers to follow the IGP shortest path without local overrides.

A Node-SID identifies a router. An Anycast-SID directs traffic toward the closest router in an anycast group, whose members must advertise the same prefix and SID value. An Adj-SID directs traffic from its advertising router through a particular adjacency or set of adjacencies, even when that overrides the normal shortest-path choice.

In SR-MPLS, a Prefix-SID must not be assigned to different prefixes. Using an anycast segment without identical SRGBs in the group can cause misrouting.
sections.plainLanguage: IGP segments can direct traffic toward a prefix, a router, an anycast group, or a particular link. Each type tells routers a different part of the path.

sections.title: BGP Segments and Binding SIDs
sections.content:
BGP can advertise a BGP-Prefix segment for a BGP route. BGP peering segments let an ingress border router steer traffic toward an egress router and a selected peer. The RFC defines PeerNode, PeerAdj, and PeerSet segments.

A Binding SID (BSID) is associated with an SR Policy. When a router receives a packet whose active segment is that BSID, it steers the packet onto the associated policy. The policy's segment list needs to be stored only on nodes that impose the policy.

If the policy changes, the node or nodes that impose it can be updated without changing users that send traffic toward the binding segment.
sections.plainLanguage: A Binding SID is a single identifier for an SR Policy. The router that owns the policy uses it to select the full segment list.

sections.title: Trust and Boundary Filtering
sections.content:
By default, SR operates inside a trusted domain, and traffic must be filtered at the domain boundaries. Routers should accept labels or SIDs only when advertised by trusted sources, using the security mechanisms of existing control-plane protocols.

Boundary routers must filter external traffic addressed to segments inside the domain. Explicit routing information must not leak across the administered domain's boundaries.

If the trust model fails or these protections are missing, the RFC identifies malicious looping, evasion of access controls, and hiding the source of denial-of-service attacks as possible problems. The document does not add new congestion-control requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted nodes should add or advertise segments. Boundary routers must block outside traffic that targets internal segment identifiers.

sections.title: Monitoring Paths and Managing Identifiers
sections.content:
Because the packet carries its path instead of signaling it through a separate protocol, operators need tools to check path operation, liveness, and performance. The architecture reduces the amount of state transit routers need to manage.

Each global segment must use a unique index or address within the SR domain. Operators need to manage these allocations carefully to avoid misrouting, and implementations should resolve detected conflicts deterministically.

In SRv6, segment identifiers are IPv6 addresses managed through the corresponding address-management mechanisms. The destination address identifies the active segment, while the routing header carries the path list.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need to monitor paths because the packet carries its route. They must also prevent two global segments from receiving the same identifier.
